 Ashlee Gabrysch, who has resigned as Chicago’s chief financial officer, answers a question during a Committee on License and Consumer Protection hearing at City Hall on Sept. 9, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) 
 By Alice Yin | ayin@chicagotribune.com | Chicago Tribune and A.D. Quig | aquig@chicagotribune.com | Chicago Tribune PUBLISHED: November 13, 2026 at 8:30 AM CST | UPDATED: November 14, 2026 at 5:03 PM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Mayor Brandon Johnson’s chief financial officer resigned Friday after just three months on the job, saying she was unable to fulfill her obligation to provide “complete and accurate” statements about the city’s finances.
 Ashlee Gabrysch exits her post as Johnson’s election-year budget is stalled thanks to an ongoing stalemate with aldermen. In her resignation letter, obtained by the Tribune, Gabrysch signaled she was leaving due to concerns over how the city was representing financial information.
 “The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about the City’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate,” Gabrysch, who was most recently a senior director at Fitch Ratings, wrote to Johnson. “I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve.”
 Johnson said “No” when asked Saturday if his team ever directed his CFO to present inaccurate financial data.
 “I can’t speak for someone else’s intentions; I can only speak to the work that I’ve done,” the mayor said at his West Side campaign office opening. “My budget is a fair budget. It’s a balanced budget. And again, I can’t speak to any of her claims or assertions.”
 The mayor now heads into month two of his fourth budget cycle without a permanent CFO. Comptroller Michael Belsky, also a Fitch alum, will step in as the acting CFO for now.
 Meanwhile, Johnson’s Finance Committee chair, Ald. Pat Dowell, who has since become a leader of the council opposition against his budget, said Friday there must be an independent financial audit of the city by an outside firm in response to Gabrysch’s allegations in her resignation letter. She was echoed by Ald. Bill Conway, 34th, who called for “an immediate and robust investigation.”
 “I call for an audit of the city finances at this point,” Dowell, 3rd, said. “I’m just shocked. … This is a sad day. Ashlee was really a good CFO.”
 In her Friday statement to the Tribune, Gabrysch said, “The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about city finances are not idle chatter. … The CFO must act scrupulously to ensure they are always accurate and complete.”
 “Throughout my career, I have remained committed to upholding the highest standards of financial integrity and transparency, and in my short time as Chief Financial Officer, I have faithfully discharged this duty,” Gabrysch said. “It has become apparent, however, that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations.”
 In a statement, Belsky said he was “disappointed” to learn about Gabrysch’s resignation, but “in my time with the City, the Mayor and his team have been extremely transparent, open, and honest with the public and City Council about the City’s fiscal position. Any suggestion to the contrary is simply incorrect.”
 Johnson’s first fiscal chief, Jill Jaworski, resigned at the start of this year. Acting CFO Steven Mahr then exited in July. The city does not yet have a permanent budget director, either. Jonathan Ernst has been serving as acting director since Annette Guzman resigned in August.
 According to correspondence obtained by the Tribune, Gabrysch last month raised concerns about the deficit reporting and characterization of the settlement borrowing with the budget and finance teams, as well as the city’s Law Department.
 Johnson’s budget team estimated next year’s budget gap at $882 million in the deficit forecast rollout in September. When Johnson formally introduced his budget last month, that number had shrunk to $652 million — an “adjusted” figure that the administration largely attributed to plans to borrow for the cost of police settlements.
 With settlement borrowing removed from the city’s deficit, Johnson claimed 76% of his gap-filling proposals were structural — which Gabrysch publicly broke with the mayor on during the first day of budget hearings.
 The newly obtained emails show on the Sunday before, she informed Johnson’s intergovernmental affairs chief, Emily Melbye, along with Pacione-Zayas and External Affairs chief Kennedy Bartley, how she would be presenting the budget figures.
 “These are the terms of my testimony, not open for revision,” Gabrysch wrote, per a copy of the Oct. 25 email. “I want to be direct about why. I am seriously concerned about the risk to the City, to the professionals in the City’s finance offices, and to me personally.”
 Gabrysch wrote that she did not want to present the city’s fiscal condition “in any way that is inaccurate or incomplete.”
 Doing so would risk a downgrade from ratings “that already sit at or near the bottom of investment grade, higher borrowing costs on every future issuance, loss of investor confidence, impaired market access, and possible regulatory action,” she said. Regulators, she noted, had individually charged public officials for misleading statements about municipal finance.
 Public press releases, media statements or posted materials from municipal authorities — not just formal documents — that include untrue statements or that omit material facts could be considered violations of federal antifraud provisions, according to Securities and Exchange Commission guidance.
 She continued, “I will not use campaign framing or political messaging in my testimony. Doing so would be inconsistent with my fiduciary responsibility as Chief Financial Officer and could put the City in legal jeopardy.”
 In a response to Gabrysch days later, Sheila Bedi, Johnson’s chief strategy officer, denied the administration ever instructed her to “misrepresent information, obscure financial realities, or repeat campaign framing.”
 “Rather, like all department heads, you were asked to discuss the Mayor’s proposed budget in the context of the administration’s governing priorities,” Bedi said, including “ensuring that working families are not asked to shoulder a disproportionate share of the City’s financial challenges. This is a reasonable expectation of senior officials.”
 Bedi requested a meeting in person, per the email, which was copied to Johnson’s acting corporation counsel, Renee Hatcher, Pacione-Zayas, Bartley and Melbye.
 In a statement on Friday, Johnson press secretary Allison Novelo said the administration had been clear about the cost of settlements in its budget forecast in September, as well as the scope of the deficit and the city’s intention to borrow to cover settlements in its public budget overview documents and presentations to the City Council last month.
 Novelo also alleged Gabrysch was absent during the budget preparation process and that she had ethical lapses of her own.
 “Her decision to direct the City Treasurer to issue a $75 million payment without proper legal authority or following the required processes raises serious concerns,” Novelo wrote. “We will refer the matter to the City’s Office of Inspector General for independent review.”
 The City Council this month voted 44-6 to approve a $75 million payment from the sale of the parking meter system to go toward the city’s pensions — a veto-proof margin. But Hatcher warned Gabrysch in a letter afterward that her direction to the city treasurer’s office for that use was “premature.”
 In response, Gabrysch wrote on Friday, “This effort by the administration to deflect from the serious issues at stake and attack those who attempt to hold them accountable is disappointing but not surprising.”
 Johnson, in his Saturday appearance, did not answer a question on whether reporting her after her resignation would be retaliatory. But he then walked back Novelo’s statement, saying his administration will not, in fact, report Gabrysch to the inspector general.
 “What I’m simply saying is that the OIG has the opportunity to do a full investigation, and if the OIG decides to do that, that’s certainly his prerogative,” Johnson said. “We’re moving on from that now.”
 The CFO is typically tasked with managing the city’s debt, long-term financial planning and reporting, and relationships with ratings agencies. Gabrysch would have taken a lead role in Johnson’s proposed $480 million debt issuance to cover various settlements through 2028, including $260 million to victims of former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara .
 Key to Gabrysch’s job was working to ensure the city was not further dinged by ratings agencies, three of which delivered downgrades after last year’s budget. The agencies, which grade the city’s creditworthiness and sway the cost of borrowing, have highlighted the city’s stubborn budget gaps driven by rising pension, debt and payroll costs; fights between the mayor and council; and continued use of one-time measures to patch up deficits as major concerns.
 Justin Marlowe, director of the Center for Municipal Finance at the University of Chicago and a close watcher of the city’s finances and credit performance, said Friday, “When the person responsible for the city’s financial credibility loses confidence in the process, everyone else should take notice.”
 Gabrysch notably disputed the 76% structural fixes figure during the first day of public budget hearings, saying those settlement costs were part of the deficit and that borrowing to cover it should be counted as a one-time gap-filling measure. With both in mind, she said structural solutions made up 56% of the mayor’s proposal.
 “The 76% number comes from removing settlements and judgments from the denominator,” she said at the time. “I stick with the $882 (million) forecasted budget. … That is my denominator.”
 Ald. Marty Quinn, 13th, said he was “not surprised that the mayor may be a little disingenuous here, that seems to be his normal course.”
 Gabrysch did not respond to Quinn’s quip but moments later took a large swig of her drink.
 The mayor at the time denied any attempts by his administration to hide the ball. “Look, we were obviously incredibly transparent,” Johnson said when asked about the discrepancy last month.
 It wasn’t the first time the mayor and his CFOs have publicly disagreed. Last year, Jaworski told a Bloomberg audience ahead of Johnson’s budget introduction that a property tax increase was “likely.”
 While property tax dollars are among the most stable and predictable revenues the city can raise on its own, they have become a political third rail. Johnson rejected the idea days later.
